title: Serving: Production and Acceleration
oneLiner: To serve many users cheaply: shrink the model (fewer bits, fewer weights), let a small model guess ahead for the big one, and schedule GPU memory and work so nothing sits idle.

what.html:
Last session showed that writing each token is limited by reading memory. This session is about the fixes used in real products: quantization and pruning make the model smaller, speculative decoding produces several tokens per expensive step, and continuous batching plus paged attention keep the GPU full of useful work.

Everyday versionA busy restaurant kitchen: use smaller plates that are quicker to carry (quantization), let a junior cook prepare dishes the head chef just checks (speculative decoding), seat a new table the moment one leaves (continuous batching), and hand out shelf space in small boxes rather than whole cupboards (paged attention).

why.html:
• These choices decide what an AI product costs per answer.
  • They decide how fast the first word appears and how smoothly the rest follow.
  • Every speed trick needs a quality check.

how.title: Three levers
how.html: Shrink the model, decode smarter, and run the system better. Most deployments use all three.

how.title: Fewer bits per weight
how.html: A 1-billion-weight model takes 4 GB in 32-bit, 1 GB in 8-bit and 0.5 GB in 4-bit. Fewer bytes means faster reading, at the cost of some rounding.

how.title: Remove weights
how.html: Drop the least useful weights, then let the model recover with a little extra training. Removing whole blocks gives real speed on ordinary GPUs.

how.title: Guess ahead, check at once
how.html: A small model drafts 4 tokens; the big model checks all 4 in one step and keeps the ones it agrees with. With 80% agreement that's about 3.4 tokens per big step, with identical output quality.

how.title: Never leave a seat empty
how.html: Instead of waiting for the slowest request in a group, start a new request the moment any finishes. In a simulation this raised GPU use from 55% to 90%.

how.title: Memory in small blocks
how.html: Give each conversation cache space in 16-token blocks as it grows, instead of reserving room for the longest possible chat. Almost nothing is wasted, so many more users fit.

how.title: Measure speed and cost
how.html: Track time to first token, time per token, total tokens per second, and cost. A $2/hour GPU making 100 tokens per second costs about $5.56 per million tokens.

demo.html: Match each description to the serving technique.

example.html:
Cost arithmetic. 100 tokens per second × 3,600 seconds = 360,000 tokens per hour. $2 ÷ 0.36 million ≈ $5.56 per million tokens. Batching to 2,000 tokens per second brings that to about 28 cents.

Supplementary When many users share the same long system prompt, its cached blocks can be reused, so that part of the prompt is almost free after the first request.

takeaways: Levers: compress the model, decode smarter, run the system better.
Quantization: 4 → 1 → 0.5 GB per 1B params; watch outliers, use group scales.
Pruning: structured for real speed; prune → recover → quantize.
Speculative decoding: (1 − α^(k+1))/(1 − α) tokens per pass, same outputs.
Continuous batching, chunked prefill and paged KV keep GPUs full; cost = price ÷ tokens.
thirty: Efficient serving pulls three levers. Model compression: quantization stores weights as b-bit integers with scales (1B params: 4 GB fp32 → 1 GB int8 → 0.5 GB int4), with per-group scales and calibration to handle outliers; pruning removes weights (unstructured needs sparse kernels; structured shrinks matrices), usually followed by recovery fine-tuning, quantization and evaluation. Algorithms: speculative decoding drafts k tokens with a cheap model and verifies them in one target pass, keeping the target's exact distribution; expected tokens per pass (1 − α^(k+1))/(1 − α) (3.36 at α = 0.8, k = 4). Systems: continuous batching refills slots per step (55% → 90% utilisation in simulation); chunked prefill stops long prompts stalling decode; paged attention allocates KV in blocks via a block table, cutting waste to a few percent and enabling prefix sharing. Metrics: TTFT, TPOT, throughput, and cost per token ($2/h at 100 tok/s ≈ $5.56 per million).
